research_scope: Investigated anthropomorphism, warmth, competence, expressiveness, non-judgmental language, relational support, agency, and accessibility in digital health, behavior-change, conversational-agent, and embodied-agent research.

Included evidence from health triage, physical-activity coaching, diabetes self-management, chronic-disease self-management, mental-health/body-image support, eating-disorder prevention, human-computer trust, and official accessibility guidance.

Distinguished a visual mascot or recurring character from an embodied conversational agent. The empirical literature is stronger for conversational and embodied agents than for a static nutrition mascot, so transfers to SuperNutrition are labeled as design implications rather than direct causal evidence.

Included first-party product examples for Finch, Duolingo, Wysa, and My Diabetes Coach to identify observable character roles and interaction patterns. Market popularity claims were treated as product or brand signals, not independent proof of causal effectiveness.
Research currency: current as of 2026-08-08, with historical studies retained when they provide stronger experimental or randomized evidence.
evidence_summary: Anthropomorphic appearance and language can increase perceived anthropomorphism and social presence in health conversational agents. In a 3 x 2 within-subject experiment with 103 participants, more humanlike appearance and verbal cues increased social presence; social presence and mindless personality attributions predicted trust, and trust predicted disclosure intention, continued-use intention, and satisfaction. This supports social presence as a useful mechanism, not the claim that human likeness makes medical information more accurate. Source: https://www.jmir.org/2023/1/e44479/

Warmth and competence are complementary trust signals. An experiment on human-computer trust found that perceived warmth, meaning benevolent or non-self-serving intent, and perceived competence shaped willingness to trust a computer system. Human-robot studies similarly found positive effects of manipulated competence and warmth on anticipated trust and attributed trustworthiness. Sources: https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/digital-humanities/articles/10.3389/fdigh.2018.00014/full and https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/robotics-and-ai/articles/10.3389/frobt.2021.640444/full

A character is more credible when warmth is paired with visible competence. For SuperNutrition, warmth should be expressed through respect, patience, and acknowledgment of uncertainty, while competence should be demonstrated through cited catalog sources, assumptions, editability, and consistent reasoning. A friendly tone cannot compensate for wrong food identity or hidden assumptions.

Relational coaching can support engagement and behavior maintenance. In a randomized trial of 70 overweight adults, an animated virtual coach that set goals and provided personalized feedback helped maintain step counts while the control group declined; the end-point difference was not significant, so the result is a maintenance signal rather than proof of a large behavior-change effect. Source: https://www.jmir.org/2012/1/e1/

Qualitative evidence supports a non-judgmental role. In interviews from longitudinal relational-agent interventions for exercise and sun protection, 15 of 34 interviewed participants described the agent as less judgmental or less overbearing than a human counselor, and 22 of 34 viewed it as contributing to behavior change; repetitive and overly general interactions were also criticized. These findings are promising but self-reported and based on a small interview subset. Source: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5822036/

Human cues do not guarantee better adherence. In a 2024 field experiment with 121 participants using a text-based physical-activity intervention, working alliance was positively related to adherence, but visual cues did not improve alliance and the groups receiving visual cues had lower adherence than relational-cue-only or no-cue groups. The authors suggest that visuals may create confusion about the agent's true nature and unrealistic expectations. Source: https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38370288/

Expressiveness should be semantically aligned and restrained. Diabetes ECA research notes that facial expressions, body movement, and speech can support natural interaction, but engagement is weakened by monotonous or repetitive content and by dissonance between speech and facial or bodily behavior. A 2026 experiment with 75 participants found body posture affected satisfaction, while facial-expression effects were not significant; this is early evidence rather than a universal rule. Sources: https://mhealth.jmir.org/2020/7/e17038/ and https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1177/20552076261450307

Empathy and sympathy are generally preferred to emotionally flat health advice, but empathy must not become false authority or agreement. Experiments with a health-advice chatbot found that participants favored sympathy and empathy over unemotional advice. In body-image conversations, young adults valued private, accessible, nonjudgmental support and self-reflection, while engagement declined over time and suggestions were difficult to translate into action. Sources: https://journals.sagepub.com/doi/10.1089/cyber.2018.0110 and https://www.jmir.org/2025/1/e78829

Agency should remain with the user. Self-determination theory and digital behavior-change guidance identify autonomy, competence, and relatedness as conditions for internalized, sustained motivation. A character should invite choices, explain options, and accept refusal; it should not decide the food, upload the photo, set a health goal, or frame compliance as loyalty. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC4327440/ and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC5999061/

Eating-disorder prevention evidence supports body-neutral and body-functionality framing rather than weight moralism. A randomized chatbot trial with 700 high-risk women reduced weight and shape concerns at 3- and 6-month follow-up, and digital interventions that focus on body functionality or body neutrality show acceptability and improvements in body-image outcomes. This supports safe, evidence-based content, but it does not show that a mascot itself prevents eating-disorder risk. Sources: https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1002/eat.23662 and https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37129116/

Eating-disorder and body-image products require stronger safety boundaries than ordinary habit apps. A design study of an eating-disorder prevention chatbot documented challenges around risk detection, crisis or clinical boundaries, and avoiding harmful dieting advice; ethics commentary highlights the danger of chatbots giving weight-loss or calorie-counting guidance to vulnerable users. The character should never moralize food, reward restriction, comment on body size, or imply that weight change is a measure of worth. Sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8811687/ and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10463082/

Accessibility guidance makes motion and expressive media optional. W3C guidance recommends allowing users to disable non-essential interaction animation, respecting reduced-motion preferences, and providing pause, stop, or hide controls for moving or auto-updating content. A character must also expose equivalent text, semantics, labels, and state changes so that emotion is not conveyed only by animation, facial color, or sound. Sources: https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/animation-from-interactions and https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/pause-stop-hide.html
source_quality_and_limits: [uncertain] The strongest evidence comes from peer-reviewed experiments, randomized trials, qualitative health-agent evaluations, a 2024 adherence field experiment, and W3C accessibility guidance. Evidence is weaker for the exact question of a lovable static nutrition mascot: most studies test conversational or embodied agents, short interactions, imagined vignettes, or single behaviors. Samples are often small, convenience-recruited, highly educated, Western, or predominantly female; outcomes frequently measure perceived trust, intention, satisfaction, or self-reported adherence rather than durable clinical behavior. Body-image evidence is not interchangeable with eating-disorder treatment evidence, and studies of healthy young adults do not establish safety for people with active eating disorders. First-party brand statements are useful for identifying intended character roles but are not independent popularity or causal-effect evidence. Animal symbolism and cross-cultural acceptance remain under-tested, so the shortlist should be treated as a hypothesis for local validation rather than an evidence-backed universal ranking. Sources: https://www.jmir.org/2023/1/e44479/ ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38370288/ ; https://www.jmir.org/2025/1/e78829/ ; https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/animation-from-interactions
audience_love_signals: [uncertain] The most credible observable signals are continued use, willingness to return, perceived support, affection or appreciation in conversation, satisfaction, and adherence rather than downloads or a brand's own claim that users love a character. Duolingo's official brand guidance calls Duo its most recognizable element, recommends expressive poses, and describes a broad emotional range; its official blog says the character cast was introduced partly to make learners want to spend more time in the product. Finch's current Google Play listing positions a customizable self-care bird as a rewarding, lightweight, fun companion whose growth is tied to self-care tasks. Wysa's public materials position its penguin chatbot and human coaches as empathetic, non-judgmental support with user control over whether AI chats are shared with a coach. These are strong examples of intended appeal and product mechanics, but they are not independent estimates of love, retention, or health outcomes. Empirical health-agent signals are mixed: users often report supportive and less judgmental interactions, while repetitive content, confusing humanlike visuals, and declining novelty can reduce engagement. Sources: https://design.duolingo.com/marketing/assets ; https://blog.duolingo.com/building-character/ ; https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?gl=US&hl=en_US&id=com.finch.finch ; https://www.wysa.com/faq ; https://mhealth.jmir.org/2020/7/e17038/ ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38370288/
relevant_brand_examples: Finch: a virtual bird is cared for by completing self-care activities. The character acts as a gentle companion and reward loop, turning reflection, mood checks, breathing, and habits into care for the pet. Product fit: useful precedent for warmth and low-friction repetition, but avoid making the pet suffer or become disappointed when a user misses a meal or skips a task. Source: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?gl=US&hl=en_US&id=com.finch.finch

Duolingo Duo and the character cast: Duo is an expressive owl mascot used across product, notifications, and marketing; the official guidance emphasizes emotional range, recognizable poses, and a supportive-cheerleader identity. The brand also documents persistence and guilt-based reminders as effective for open rates and retention. Product fit: strong precedent for memorability, expression, and scalable character storytelling; safety implication: do not import shame, threat, streak anxiety, or fear of disappointing the mascot into eating or body-related behavior. Sources: https://design.duolingo.com/marketing/assets and https://design.duolingo.com/writing/duo

Wysa: a penguin represents a wellbeing chatbot framed around empathetic, non-judgmental support. Its public service materials distinguish coaching from diagnosis or treatment and allow users to opt in or out of sharing AI chats with a human coach. Product fit: useful precedent for a warm companion with explicit boundaries, privacy control, and referral to human support. Sources: https://apps.apple.com/cl/iphone/story/id1614514977?l=en-GB and https://www.wysa.com/faq

My Diabetes Coach: Laura is an embodied conversational agent in a smartphone self-management app that delivers education, feedback, and motivational support for blood-glucose monitoring, medication, activity, food, and foot care. Product fit: relevant precedent for a health coach that appears at planned support moments rather than dominating every screen. Source: https://mhealth.jmir.org/2020/7/e17038/

Relational-agent health coaching: exercise, sun-protection, physical-activity, and chronic-disease studies use recurring characters to provide personalized feedback, small talk, encouragement, and relational continuity. Product fit: supports a character as a persistent sidekick; limitation: it does not justify presenting the character as a clinician or making autonomous health decisions. Sources: https://www.jmir.org/2012/1/e1/ and https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8603169/
useful_character_traits: Warm and benevolent: communicates care through patience, respect, gratitude for user effort, and a calm response to uncertainty. Warmth should signal good intent, not emotional dependency.

Competent but bounded: shows where a food suggestion came from, names assumptions, distinguishes recognition from nutrition calculation, and says when it does not know. Competence should be visible in evidence and recovery, not in an authoritative costume or overconfident voice.

Non-judgmental and weight-neutral: never labels foods as good, bad, clean, guilty, cheating, earned, or burned; never praises restriction or uses body size as a progress score. Use body functionality, nourishment, preference, context, and self-defined goals where relevant.

Expressive but semantically aligned: use a small, legible expression set for curiosity, acknowledgment, uncertainty, apology, waiting, and celebration. Facial, textual, motion, and audio cues should agree; do not smile while presenting a failed recognition, medical warning, or privacy decision.

Agency-preserving: ask, offer, explain, and accept refusal. The companion may suggest a next step but must not silently upload, infer a serving, lock a correction, or turn a suggestion into a commitment.

Persistent without coercion: use reminders and continuity only when invited, with snooze, mute, and frequency controls. Avoid guilt, punishment, loss framing, emotional blackmail, or simulated abandonment when users disengage.

Predictable and reparative: maintain a stable voice and visual identity, acknowledge mistakes plainly, apologize without theatrics, and make correction easy. Consistency matters more than novelty for trust.

Culturally humble and inclusive: avoid a gendered, thin, athletic, young, or clinician-coded body; avoid culturally specific gestures and food assumptions; support localization and alternative text without changing the underlying evidence.

Accessible by default: provide equivalent text and semantic labels, readable contrast, static fallback, reduced-motion support, pause or stop controls, captioned audio, and no meaning that depends only on facial animation, color, or sound.
candidate_animals_or_archetypes: [uncertain] No animal is empirically established as universally lovable, trustworthy, or culturally safe for a nutrition product. Treat the following as hypotheses for co-design, not as a ranking. A small bird such as a finch or sparrow is a plausible primary direction because it suggests lightness, curiosity, everyday movement, and a non-human, non-body-coded companion; Finch provides a product precedent, but not proof that birds transfer to nutrition. A soft abstract creature or rounded field-guide companion is the safest cross-cultural baseline because it avoids animal taboos, food-chain associations, body-size symbolism, and human gender or age cues. A curious guide archetype, using a notebook or magnifying-glass metaphor sparingly, can express competence and uncertainty without claiming medical authority. An otter-like playful companion may support warmth and sociability but has little health-specific evidence. A bear, elephant, or other large-bodied animal can be affectionate but risks linking the mascot to body size, weight, appetite, or strength stereotypes; avoid unless target-user research explicitly supports it. Avoid anthropomorphic food characters that imply a meal is a friend to be eaten, a body-shaped character, a scale or calorie character, a clinician avatar, and a guilt-inducing watchdog. Sources: https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?gl=US&hl=en_US&id=com.finch.finch ; https://www.jmir.org/2023/1/e44479/ ; https://www.frontiersin.org/journals/robotics-and-ai/articles/10.3389/frobt.2021.640444/full
cultural_and_safety_risks: [uncertain] Anthropomorphic cues can raise social presence, trust, disclosure, and continued-use intention, which also raises the risk of overtrust, inappropriate disclosure, and mistaking a character for a human or clinician. Clearly disclose that the companion is digital, state what it can and cannot do, and keep privacy and remote-processing consent in a separate, explicit user-controlled flow. Eating-disorder and body-image safety risks include weight-loss framing, calorie or exercise compensation, food moralization, body transformation imagery, thin or athletic ideals, streak punishment, praise for restriction, and a pet that expresses disappointment when users do not log or comply. Use body-neutral or functionality-oriented language, do not infer health or worth from appearance, and route suspected clinical risk to appropriate professional support rather than improvising treatment. Cultural risks include animal taboos, religious or dietary associations, species-specific symbolism, gender coding, humor that does not localize, and gestures or expressions that read differently across cultures; test the visual and verbal system with intended markets. Accessibility risks include motion sickness or vestibular reactions from animation, distraction for people with attention or cognitive disabilities, flashing or blinking that can trigger seizures, low contrast, inaccessible text inside artwork, and emotional meaning conveyed only visually. Respect reduced-motion preferences, provide pause or stop controls, keep a static equivalent, expose state in text, and test with screen readers and keyboard or switch input. Sources: https://www.jmir.org/2023/1/e44479/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC8811687/ ; https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10463082/ ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37129116/ ; https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/animation-from-interactions ; https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/pause-stop-hide.html
visual_and_interaction_patterns: Use a stylized 2D or low-realism form rather than a near-human avatar. A clearly non-human character can provide warmth and social presence while avoiding uncanny realism, gendered body comparison, and false clinician authority.

Define a small state vocabulary: listening, curious, unsure, explaining, asking for confirmation, sorry, ready, and quietly celebrating a user-chosen action. Map each state to text and accessibility semantics; do not encode certainty or safety in color alone.

Show the character at decision points: before or after capture to explain the workflow, beside ambiguous candidates to ask a clarification, beside serving assumptions to invite editing, and after correction to acknowledge the user's authority. Keep it out of the camera view and do not let it obscure food evidence.

Make uncertainty an expressive strength. A calm inquisitive pose and wording such as 'I see two plausible matches; which one is closer?' should be more common than triumphant confirmation. A correction should trigger a neutral acknowledgment, not a sad or ashamed performance.

Use brief, purposeful motion only. Respect system reduced-motion settings, provide a static mode and a visible pause or stop control, avoid flashing and endless ambient movement, and never require animation to understand the food candidate, confidence, consent, or result.

Prefer user-invoked interaction over attention capture. A character can be tapped for explanation or help, but it should not chase the user across screens, interrupt camera composition, auto-play speech, or send emotionally loaded reminders.

Keep the character independent from nutrition authority. The mascot can introduce catalog provenance, assumptions, and alternatives, while the UI shows exact source, dataset version, serving basis, and editable numbers. Do not make a smile or costume substitute for evidence.

Design for scale and localization: a recognizable silhouette at icon size, a high-contrast static variant, separate text from artwork, right-to-left-safe layouts, captioned or muted audio, screen-reader labels, and expressions that do not rely on culture-specific hand gestures or facial conventions.

Use reward language tied to self-defined care or learning, not moral scores. Celebrate a user checking an assumption, adding a serving detail, or choosing a preferred alternative as an act of agency; never make the character's affection contingent on calories, weight, logging streaks, or restriction.
implication_for_supernutrition: Position the character as an honest companion and interface guide, not a nutrition judge, doctor, diet coach, or autonomous decision-maker. The product promise of honest uncertainty is compatible with a warm character only if the character visibly admits limits and hands control back to the user.

At camera capture, the character should explain what will happen and remind users that recognition may be uncertain. It must not imply that the image is already uploaded or that consent is automatic. Any remote route remains an explicit product-level consent decision, not a character-driven emotional request.

At candidate review, use the companion to ask focused questions about identity, mixed dishes, brand, recipe, oil or sauce, and serving basis. Preserve confirm, edit, search, barcode, and manual paths as first-class choices. Example: 'I am not sure whether this is lentil soup or dal. Which is closer?' Avoid 'You chose the wrong food.'

At the nutrition result, keep the character beside provenance and assumptions rather than replacing them. It may say, 'These numbers use the selected catalog item and your serving estimate; you can change either,' while the UI exposes source, dataset version, serving basis, calculation assumptions, and uncertainty.

Use a non-judgmental language policy across character copy, system notifications, and error recovery. Ban good/bad food labels, cheat or guilt language, earn/burn metaphors, punitive faces, weight-loss promises, body-size comments, and reminders that imply the user has disappointed the mascot.

Use the character to reinforce agency and correction. The most trustworthy celebration is acknowledging a user decision or a clarified assumption, not claiming that a health outcome has been achieved. Let users mute, hide, or reduce the character's motion and frequency without losing functionality.

Treat the visual layer as a modular adapter to the existing camera-first state machine: it can render capture, quality-check, consent explanation, analysis, review, correction, serving, and result states, but it must not own routing, consent, catalog authority, or cleanup. This matches SuperNutrition's ports-and-adapters and explicit user-control constraints.

For eating-disorder and body-image safety, keep the companion away from weight-loss coaching and appearance judgments. Use neutral food descriptions, body functionality and nourishment language where relevant, a calm escalation path, and professional-support links for clinical concerns. The character should never infer an eating disorder from a photo or make a medical conclusion.

Recommended default tone: warm, curious, concise, and humble. Recommended default agency: assistant with invitation, not decision-maker. Recommended default expressiveness: low-to-moderate, stateful, and optional. Recommended default form: clearly non-human, gender-neutral, non-body-coded, and scalable to a static accessible icon. Sources: https://www.jmir.org/2023/1/e44479/ ; https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38370288/ ; https://www.w3.org/WAI/WCAG22/Understanding/animation-from-interactions
recommendation: Primary direction: prototype a clearly non-human 'curious field guide' companion, with a small-bird or soft abstract-creature skin tested as variants. The underlying character contract should be warmth plus demonstrated competence plus explicit humility, not a fixed animal claim.

Keep the character visually simple, expressive, and non-body-coded: rounded silhouette, inclusive neutral palette, a small set of semantic expressions, static fallback, and no clinician uniform, scale, measuring tape, body transformation, or food-moralizing symbolism.

Make agency a core design rule: the companion asks and explains, while the user confirms identity, serving, remote consent, and corrections. The companion cannot create urgency, punish a missed action, or imply that trust means surrendering control.

Borrow from Finch's care-companion loop, My Diabetes Coach's scheduled support moments, Wysa's explicit wellbeing boundaries, and Duolingo's expressive character system. Do not borrow Duolingo's guilt or threat-based retention tactics for nutrition or body-related behaviors.

Treat high anthropomorphism as an experiment, not the default. Compare a no-character baseline, a low-realism warm companion, and a more expressive bird or pet skin with identical health content. Choose the version that improves calibrated trust, comprehension, correction behavior, and willingness to return without increasing shame, over-disclosure, or false confidence.

Do not finalize the animal or use 'lovable' as a success criterion until target-user testing covers cultural fit, people with disabilities, people with body-image concerns or eating-disorder lived experience through an appropriate safety-led process, and users who prefer no character. Sources: https://design.duolingo.com/marketing/assets ; https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?gl=US&hl=en_US&id=com.finch.finch ; https://www.wysa.com/faq ; https://mhealth.jmir.org/2020/7/e17038/
validation_plan: Phase 1, formative co-design: recruit 18 to 24 compensated target users across ordinary nutrition-app users, users with accessibility needs, and people with lived experience of body-image or eating concerns through clinician or advocacy partners. Include a no-character preference option and do not ask participants to disclose diagnoses in the product task.

Test three visually matched prototypes with identical recognition and nutrition content: no character, warm abstract field-guide companion, and small-bird or pet companion. Randomize order. Include camera capture, ambiguous-food review, serving correction, remote-consent explanation, and a result with visible assumptions.

Measure calibrated trust rather than trust alone: perceived warmth, perceived competence, perceived judgment, social presence, willingness to continue, willingness to disclose, understanding of AI identity and limits, recognition of uncertainty, successful correction, consent comprehension, user-reported agency, and task completion. Add a short body-image and shame-safety check after food-related tasks.

Run an accessibility pass in the same study: screen reader and semantic-label tasks, large text and contrast, keyboard or switch navigation where applicable, reduced-motion and static modes, muted audio, captions, and pause or stop controls. Success requires equivalent task completion without animation or audio.

Set go or no-go thresholds before testing: the character must not reduce uncertainty recognition, consent comprehension, correction success, or user control versus the no-character baseline; it should not increase shame, body dissatisfaction, perceived surveillance, or pressure to comply; and any engagement lift must survive removal of guilt-based language.

Phase 2, only after safety gates pass: a 2-week diary or pilot with a larger sample comparing return rate, correction rate, muted or hidden-character rate, user-initiated help, and repeated-meal completion. Treat this as engagement and calibration evidence, not proof of clinical eating or weight outcomes.
